instructions:
Voice Affect: calm, curious and clear.
Tone: conversational mathematical teaching for a bright sixteen-year-old.
Pacing: steady and unhurried, with pauses around counting examples.
Pronunciation: Heesch is heesh; Bašić is BAH-shich, written Bashich in the spoken script.
Delivery: no imitation of any person or branded presentation style.

clips.text: Take this marked hexagon and surround it with matching copies. One complete ring fits. Then another, then a third. How long can a shape keep growing before the next ring becomes impossible? That is the question behind a Heesch number.

A ring is called a corona. Here, complete means that the new cluster fully encloses the old one, with no overlaps, holes, or point pinches. The union must be a solid disk-like region. These strict rules matter when checking a picture.

A shape that tiles the entire plane can keep growing indefinitely. A non-tiling shape may still surround itself several times. The challenge is to distinguish an impressive patch from the largest number of rings that any permitted construction can achieve.

This study asks a bounded version of that question. Fix one of thirty-four small base shapes. Give each boundary edge one centred bump, nick, or flat mark. Keep rotated, reflected and translated copies on the prescribed square or hexagonal grid.

A bump must fit a nick, while a flat edge meets another flat edge. Two bumps collide, and a nick facing a flat edge leaves a forbidden gap. These matching rules turn an ordinary shape into a jigsaw-like piece.

Our single-hexagon witness has three bumps, two nicks, and one flat edge. Bumps outnumber nicks by one. Such a marking is called unbalanced. We search over every unbalanced marking, not only this particular arrangement.

When two pieces meet correctly, an internal bump and nick cancel in the count. Each copy still contributes one net surplus bump. In a finite patch, that uncancelled surplus has to be carried by the outer boundary.

For larger and larger patches, the number of pieces grows like area, while the boundary capacity grows like perimeter. Eventually the surplus cannot fit. The written geometric argument makes this precise for the curved pieces, showing that an unbalanced piece cannot tile the plane.

Now build the actual three-ring witness from its retained placements. Start with one central piece, then add six, twelve, and eighteen. That gives thirty-seven pieces in total. Every displayed orientation comes from the checked witness, not an invented decorative pattern.

For a single hexagon, a hypothetical fourth ring would contain sixty-one hexagons altogether. Its outside has only fifty-four edges. Each unbalanced piece contributes at least one surplus mark, so the patch would need room for at least sixty-one.

Sixty-one cannot fit into fifty-four slots. That is the classical counting obstruction credited to Epstein. Three rings are attained, and four are impossible. Larger base pieces have more complicated boundaries, so this simple count no longer settles their best markings.

Consider a straight row of four hexagons. It has eighteen outer edges. The retained optimal witness uses nine bumps, eight nicks, and one flat edge. Around the boundary they form a block of bumps, a flat, then a block of nicks.

Place the exact central row, then its first ring. The cluster now contains twenty-four underlying hexagonal cells. Add the second ring and there are sixty-eight cells. Each whole marked row counts as one piece, so cells and pieces are different counts.

Continue with the third, fourth and fifth rings. The total cell counts become one hundred and sixty, three hundred and sixteen, and five hundred and twenty-four. Dividing the last count by four gives one hundred and thirty-one pieces.

This picture proves that this marking reaches at least five rings. It does not by itself show that another marking cannot reach six. The new question is a maximum over all unbalanced choices of the eighteen edge labels.

Each edge has three labels, so eighteen edges give three to the eighteenth possibilities: more than three hundred and eighty-seven million assignments before restrictions and symmetries. Checking each marking separately would repeat much of the same geometric work.

Instead, make both the marking and the placements part of one yes-or-no puzzle. A switch says whether a placement is used. Other switches choose its edge labels. Rules forbid overlap, enforce matching, and require the requested surrounding layers.

This is a satisfiability problem, often shortened to SAT. All the switches must obey all the rules simultaneously. One additional counting rule requires at least one surplus bump. Swapping bumps and nicks covers the opposite imbalance in the lattice model.

The window is finite for a reason. A piece in the next ring must touch the preceding cluster, so it cannot jump arbitrarily far away. The paper proves a distance bound for every layer. The search window contains every possible patch at the requested depth.

A yes answer comes with actual placements and marks. A separate short program reconstructs the patch, checks matching and overlap, and checks that each growing union is a disk enclosing the previous union. The saved geometry is the witness we animate.

A no answer needs a different receipt. The solver writes a sequence of logical proof steps, called a DRAT proof. A separate checker verifies that those steps establish inconsistency of the encoded puzzle. The written encoding argument connects that puzzle back to rings.

For the straight four-row, five rings have a witness and six are excluded for every unbalanced marking. The same maximum of five holds for the straight five-row. These are exact maxima in the stated lattice model, not upper bounds for arbitrary off-grid arrangements.

The full ledger covers thirty-four bases: twelve shapes made from at most four hexagons, twenty-one made from at most five squares, plus the straight five-hexagon row. Every entry has a checked witness and a verified upper-bound proof record.

For straight hexagon rows of lengths one through five, the maxima are three, four, four, five, and five. Among the twelve bases of at most four hexagons, only the straight four-row reaches five. The non-straight shapes reach at most three.

For the square-cell bases, the maximum is three, achieved by the straight rows of four and five squares. The other values are one or two. Six non-row optimal witnesses have imbalance two or three, so the row pattern does not describe every optimum.

The checks also try deliberately broken witnesses. One hundred and seventy mutations are rejected. A second encoder agrees on both tested bounds for thirty-two bases, excluding the two largest row cases. These cross-checks support the model without pretending every implementation is formally verified.

Now separate this result from the planar record. Mann already constructed five-ring hexapillars, and the Heesch Number Atlas lists five for particular markings of the four- and five-rows. This package does not announce a new five-ring example or a new record.

Its narrower contribution is the maximum over all unbalanced single-slot markings, with replayable lower and upper evidence. Possible overlap with Mann and Thomas's smaller tables remains unresolved because their full text was unavailable. Novelty is therefore qualified.

Bojan Bashich's published six-ring construction is a separate existing result. Here is its retained geometry: one hundred and sixty-nine copies. The package audits that published patch exactly, including the strict no-hole and no-pinch requirements. It confirms the construction rather than extending it.

Watch the six layers arrive in order. They contain six, ten, thirteen, thirty-two, fifty-two, and fifty-five pieces around the centre. At each stage, the boundary was checked as one simple closed cycle, so a pinched drawing cannot quietly pass as a valid disk.

The upper-bound proof files for the largest puzzles were checked in completed runs. The retained package stores their hashes, commands and verification logs; it does not ship every large proof file. No claim is made that video production replayed those expensive proofs.

Remember the boundary of the result. One centred mark per edge. Unbalanced markings. Strict coronas. Copies on the prescribed lattice. More mark slots, balanced non-tilers, or copies sliding off that lattice are different questions. No global off-grid upper bound is established here.

The proof pattern has two halves. A concrete picture shows what can be built. A checked impossibility proof rules out the next layer for every allowed marking. Combining them turns a successful construction into an exact maximum within a clearly specified model.

Nothing here establishes a planar Heesch number of seven. Correctness confidence is high inside the lattice model; novelty is more limited. The paper, retained witnesses and editable scenes accompany this video. Narration uses a synthetic voice.
